#4163. The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Switch 2 Updated (Version 1.1.1), Here Are The Patch Notes

Update [Wed 4th Nov 2026, 12:45pm]: The official patch notes have now gone live for Version 1.1.1 of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2.

It adds support for the Switch mobile app Zelda Notes and also fixes several issues to improve the overall game experience. Here's the rundown courtesy of Nintendo's Japanese support page:

After updating the software, please follow the instructions displayed at the start of the game to set up "ZELDA NOTES."

As Nintendo has previously explained, Zelda Notes allows you to see a record of your accomplishments, test your knowledge of the game, create and share your own ocarina melodies, and more. You don't need a Switch Online membership to use it, either.

You can find out the file size of this update and other information in the original story below:

Original Story: Some parts of the world are now just hours away from the launch of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2, and ahead of this, Nintendo has rolled out a new game update.

The anticipated release has been bumped from Version 1.0.0 to Version 1.1.1. Next time you check your game, you should be prompted to update. We had a look and can confirm our copy is also running on Version 1.1.1.

Based on the "manage software" section in the Switch 2 option menu, the remake is now 24.8GB in size, and this latest update is around 343MB to install. There are no patch notes just yet, but when we get an update about what's included, we'll let you know.

"Day one" and pre-release updates like this are pretty standard for Nintendo games nowadays, with the company often rolling them out to activate certain online features such as multiplayer. Star Fox also got a day one update when it returned earlier this year. Apart from overhauled graphics and gameplay updates, this latest remake includes support for amiibo and the Switch app Zelda Notes.

Again, if we hear any updates about this latest patch, we'll let you know. Have you been prompted to update your copy of Ocarina of Time yet? Have you got it digitally downloaded and ready to go, or are you picking up a physical copy? Let us know in the comments.

#4162. The Sims 4 patch makes it so your public lot gatherings won't be interrupted by rogue Sims

Stranger Sims will no longer just crash your public lot events in The Sims 4 to talk about whatever.

The Sims 4 will soon get a new update to resolve a number of issues, some of which have long caused headaches for players. The latest update will arrive March 17 on PC and Mac, followed by PlayStation and Xbox at an unspecified time later.

Outside of the fixes themselves, the patch also makes good on the recent re-commitment to continue improving quality of life for players, so there’s plenty here longtime players will appreciate.

In the latest episode of The Sims 4’s Laundry List blog series, where the developer goes through the most reported problems with the game and how it plans to solve them, we got a rundown of what to expect from next week’s patch.

You can look forward to five major fixes in this one, but arguably the most important is a change to how Sims determine who they speak with on a lot. This is especially relevant for public lots, where Sims would sometimes interrupt ongoing conversations by barging in and starting a conversation with your Sim.

Going forward, Sims will prioritise familiar Sims with whom they already have rapport, and be less likely to latch onto strangers. If you’ve witnessed a date your Sim was on get interrupted because of that, you’ll certainly appreciate the change.

Speaking of budding romance, Prom is coming back to in-game Calendars, and Sims can once again attend. Maxis said this will work with new and existing saves, and that you should also expect Prom goals to be completable once again.

Pets and animals get some love in this patch, too. First, pets and horses will no longer get lost in Premade Households. The fix prevents that from happening in new saves, but if you already had that happen to you in your current save, it’ll still be there.

You may now also assign animals to an Animal Shed after moving your house to a new lot, so you hopefully won’t be confused as to why they’re stuck in your inventory. This fix applies to existing saves as well as new ones.

Lower down the list of urgent fixes is an update that makes it so Sims’ eye blinking will show fully closed eyes for most interactions. The upcoming patch also comes with a host of Sims autonomy fixes, including one that prevents them from excessively flirting with each other.

Catch up on the full list at the link near the top of the page. And, in case you missed it, Maxis recently announced that The Sims 4 will soon get paid mods, something that many in the community are skeptical about.

#4161. HELENA : Cloud District is a megastructure photography game laser targeted at my interests, and it's out next week

Yes, I'm doing it, I'm writing about a megastructure game for the second time this week because come on, HELENA : Cloud District just looks stunning, don't it? Admittedly there's a chance you've not heard of it, that be the way of things in this algorithmically dominated world, but allow me to tell you about its big, scary world and the strange camera you're equipped with to capture all the sights it holds.

In the world of HELENA : Cloud District, you have come across a rotting megastructure that appears to be long abandoned, all sorts of strange flora dotted throughout it. In one part, it's something of a precision first-person platformer, as you navigate its intricately layered world with drops so steep you'd probably die before you hit the bottom. At the centre of it all is a computer, and it's here where you must bring all of your photographs in order to learn more about the history of the place.

The in-game camera itself is a fascinating thing to look at, completely impossible, alien and ancient in its design. From what I can tell it's a sort of metallic helmet, these insect-like segments snapping into place when you're gearing up to take a snap. You only appear to have three photo slots at any given point in time, meaning you can't just go gallivanting around the place all trigger happy like. There's an amount of care you have to put in positioning yourself and subsequently finding your way back to the central computer.

It's non-linear too, there's no set path you have to take, and it seems like there's some neat movement mechanics too. "Slide, hover, and glide through the structure in your own creative way in order to reach every level and get deeper into the slumbering Cloud District," explains the game's Steam page. Sounds like you don't have to worry too much about that falling to your death thing, then. I'm quite enthused by what HELENA : Cloud District is putting down, and it has a release date now too: October 29th. Same day as Hypnos! I now dub October 29th megastructure day. There will not be a vote on this matter. Ahead of HELENA's release, make sure to give it a wishlist on Steam.

#4160. Former Xbox Manager Explains Why $500M Cost For Gears: E-Day Doesn't Tell The Whole Story

Update [Mon 2nd Nov 2026, 1pm]: Windows Central's Jez Corden has weighed in with a few extra details this morning as well, explaining that according to a "variety of trusted sources", The Coalition has been contributing to many other Xbox projects over the past 6-7 years.

All of these seemingly factor into the $500M budget that has been attributed, although it's unknown to what extent.

"...The Coalition worked for over a year and a half on a prototype project for Xbox that Windows Central understands was ultimately canceled. The Coalition also worked on Avowed, Hellblade 2, Clockwork Revolution, State of Decay 3, Grounded and Grounded 2, and has even contributed to the upcoming StarCraft reboot."

"The Coalition also spent a great deal of time working with Epic Games on the "Matrix Awakens" Unreal Engine demonstration, as well as the Alpha Point demo, both of which were intended to showcase the potential of UE5 on next-gen consoles and PCs."

Nevertheless, Corden warns that $500 million is a "lot of money to invest without a specific structure in place to explain why some of these costs were worthwhile to Microsoft auditors", and that there have even been "some internal disagreements over how exactly attribution should be distributed".

Original Story: Over the past couple of weeks, there's been a lot of chatter about a rumoured $500 million cost for The Coalition to make Gears of War: E-Day, alongside debates about how much of that money went on the game itself.

Speaking on the weekend, former Xbox exec Derek Reese shared his take on the situation, suggesting that The Coalition is heavily involved with supporting Microsoft's branch of the Unreal Engine, which is where a lot of the cost goes.

Here's what the ex-Senior Product Manager of Xbox Game Services had to say:

So much of that cost is The Coalition being on the hook for the Microsoft branch of Unreal and one of the flagship titles. I should know, I tried to get leadership to support a plan to have other studios adopt it and write off the support costs. Same problem with Turn10 and ForzaTech.

This aligns with what Jez Corden of Windows Central was saying a few weeks ago as well, who originally suggested that because The Coalition is "the technological glue for all of Xbox", some of that money is "spread across the entire portfolio" and even goes towards The Coalition's help on other Xbox games like Fable and Forza Horizon.

Corden confirmed yesterday that Reese's comments align with what he's heard:

In some follow-up posts, Reese mentioned that he thinks The Coalition "accomplished their end goals very well and delivered a great accomplishment in E-Day", while also suggesting that there's a "publicly visible pattern of allowing departments to shoulder the costs of leadership direction", pointing to Double Fine as a recent notable example.

So, hopefully we can put this one to bed now! It seems the $500 million budget IS a legit figure for Gears of War: E-Day, but it's hard to realistically attribute that entire figure to the game itself.

The big question is what Xbox thinks about all of this, including whether the game has been a success in terms of sales, Premium Upgrade conversions, Xbox Game Pass subscriptions and its pulling power as an Xbox console exclusive, and it could be some time until we know the answer to that.

#4159. Crimson Desert PC specs don't keep resolution and framerate targets a secret, and they don't use upscaling for everything either

Finally, a PC specification list that actually indicates resolution and framerate targets, and doesn't leave console players behind.

Crimson Desert is a little over one week away from release, and developer Pearl Abyss has delivered the official, final list of specs for the game. The twist is that the specs not only include useful information for PC players, they also cover similarly relevant details for console players, who traditionally don’t get mentioned in those reveals.

The specs are decently detailed, but more surprisingly - except for a single instance - they don’t include upscaling on PC, another thing games have gotten too comfortable using, even with their lowest specs.

On the official Crimson Desert website, developer Pearl Abyss has delivered a chunky post breaking down five different sets of PC requirements for the upcoming open-world action RPG. Each set indicates the graphics preset being used - and crucially, the resolution and framerate targets you can expect with each.

With the exception of the Minimum spec, all other presets do not appear to rely on upscaling of any kind. They do not say, however, whether ray tracing is being used with any of them, which is a feature that will throw all of those specs out of whack.

That same transparency also extends to non-PC platforms, which traditionally get few, if any, details about their own resolution and framerate targets. The console set of specs are extensive, just like PC, covering both PlayStation, and Xbox.

It’s granular enough to indicate which upscaling tech is being used, where applicable. This is relevant for owners of a PS5 Pro, a console that has access to Sony’s PSSR upscaling, alongside the standard AMD FSR tech the base console - and Xbox - use.

The developer has also revealed the base resolution for each mode across each console, and the resolution the image will be upscaled to using whichever tech is being utilised.

And, if you’re one of the five people who play games on Mac, you’ll be thrilled to know that the specs also include a section for Mac devices, split between the different Mac chips. The quality preset being used with each is not clear, however.

Finally, there's a set of specs for the Rog Xbox Ally, covering both the X and S models.

Crimson Desert arrives March 20 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. You can expect more coverage from us at release and beyond.

#4158. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs. People called them RPGs": Gloomwood's publisher isn't too keen on using the term immersive sim despite it being one

You know, I think at this point in my life there is a non-zero chance I will die before anyone is able to settle comfortably on what defines an immersive sim. I'm not going to even try to! The idea is too annoying and I'm sure someone will disagree with some aspect of it. And if you ask New Blood boss Dave Oshry, when it comes to trying to flog an immersive sim, it's probably best to not even refer to it as one.

"Is it a good marketing term? No. It sucks," Oshry told PC Gamer in a recent interview. "It's awful." For those unfamiliar with New Blood, they're a publisher of some pretty cultishly popular games like ULTRAKILL, as well as immersive sims like Gloomwood and Fallen Aces. Ironically, though, it's through publishing Gloomwood and working with lead dev Dillon Rogers specifically that he even heard of the term. "He's like, 'That's what these are called'. I'm like, 'I have never heard that before in my life. What the fuck are you talking about?'"

That doesn't mean Oshry had never heard of or played an imsim before, he was familiar with classics like Deus Ex, he just considered them to be a different genre: RPGs. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs. People called them RPGs. That's the funny thing about an immersive sim. You're immersed in this world. You're building your character. Yeah, that's called an RPG, brother. That's a roleplaying game." Perhaps a controversial statement amongst the diehard imsim fans, but perhaps not an entirely untrue statement either.

In Oshry's opinion, "if you market something as an RPG, I think you'll do better than marketing it as an immersive sim." This part I'm not sure I'd entirely agree with. Sure, everyone knows what an RPG is, but they do also have certain expectations that come with them, such as stats and the like that you don't typically find in imsims. Ahah! Maybe that's the difference. Immersive sims are RPGs without the stats. By golly, I've done it without even trying. Either way, this Oshry fellow does seem to be pretty good at peddling weird little indies, so maybe I should just pipe down.

#4156. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with a decent selection of maps and modes

Battlefield 6's second-ever free trial, and the first in 2026, is upon us.

Battlefield Studios has announced that Battlefield 6 is going free to play for one week next week. Well, a portion of the game is, anyway, as part of a free trial that will include some of the game’s most popular modes and maps.

Though it does not encompass the entirety of the game, the free trial is fairly generous. Here’s what to expect.

For starters, the trial kicks off Tuesday, March 17 and will run until the following Tuesday, March 24. The trial will be accessible from Battlefield Redsec, the already free-to-play portion of the game.

Once downloaded, you’ll find a new Battlefield 6 Free Trial section in the main menu. Because Redsec and Battlefield 6 multiplayer share progression, if you played the former at any point, you’ll be able to pick up from where you left off.

The same is also true the other way around; if this is your first time with Battlefield 6, all your unlocks will carry over to the full version, as well as to Redsec if you decide stick with the free-to-play off-shoot.

Once it kicks off, you’ll find three playlists to choose from. Casual Breakthrough, All-out Warfare, and a third playlist showcasing the new Nightfall game mode and its associated map.

All-out Warfare is what you come to Battlefield for, and that playlist features Conquest, Breakthrough, as well as BF6’s newcomer Escalation - all large-scale, combined arms game modes. They will be playable across four maps. You get to play on two from Season 2: Contaminated, and Hagental Base, one from Season 1: Eastwood, and Mirak Valley from the base game.

Casual Breakthrough is based on a playlist that already exists in the core game, and it’s really designed as a nice on-ramp for new players. It also offers less intense gameplay, perfect for people grinding unlocks.

Casual Breakthrough is limited to just 16 real players (eight per team), with the rest filled up with bots. You earn the same amount of XP in those matches, except when you interact with bots, so killing a bot will net less than a human player. Outside of that, unlocks, Challenges and all other things that don’t depend on stat-tracking can be done within.

In the trial, the Casual Breakthrough playlist includes Hagental Base, Contaminated, and Eastwood.

The most interesting is the third playlist, in part because its content will also be available to owners of the full game for the first time right alongside free-to-play players. Nightfall is a playlist exclusive to the Hagental Base map.

This is a very small map, so the mode selection here is Team Deathmatch, Squad Deathmatch, and Domination. Under Nightfall conditions, lights across the entire map are turned off, so you’re going to have use your NVGs to be able to see. This is also a god opportunity to try out weapon attachments that specifically work under low-light conditions, which typically don’t get much use in multiplayer.

March 17 also marks the launch of the second stage of Battlefield 6’s Season 2, which comes with the aforementioned Nightfall content, as well as a big new update - so the timing works out nicely for everyone.

#4155. Abelina is a strange, platforming romp through a natural afterlife from a former League of Legends animator and the composer of Zach Cregger's Resident Evil

Would that make what we're currently in the beforedeath?

I have no particular thoughts on what the afterlife may look like, namely because if there is one, and I'm allowed to hang out in it, I don't want to be disappointed. What if I have the expectation that it's a hedonistic paradise and am met with only having a guy named Gary who only eats cheese sandwiches for company? How embarrassing! No, I'll leave the imagining to others on this particular front. Doing so bears some ripe fruit for me occasionally, too, as is the case today with Abelina, a surreal platformer about a man who died and finds himself tending to gardens and carving masks and trying "not to think about what this place might really be."

My immediate reaction upon seeing Abelina is that it has the vibe of a Soviet stop motion film only Letterboxd users have heard of, which is perhaps the highest compliment I can give to a game graphically. In it, you play as Vasily, who "died a while ago." He finds himself in the titular Abelina, an odd, nature-filled afterlife, where he's been trying to find happiness again with a small handful of other folks doing the same.

I don't think Abelina is a puzzle game, but it does look like you have to put some thought into your platforming at points. There is flying to be done, dungbeetle-esque rolling, precise jumps to be made. It seems the entire thing is about navigating this otherworldly locale, and hopefully finding some truth amongst it all. You may not always find the correct path, with branching paths and open vistas seemingly offering a multitude of ways forward, all while being led by a "mysterious rabbit-cat."

It's also a game with some skill behind it, being led by Gabe Askew, who's worked on CG cinematics for the likes of Valorant, League of Legends and Love, Death + Robots. Sonically we should be in for a pleasant time too, as Weapons and the recent Resident Evil movie's composer Ryan Holladay is on the soundtrack for Abelina. I'm curious about what else it has to offer and am keen to get my hands on it to see how that platforming feels. In the meantime, you might join me by wishlisting it on Steam ahead of its release in 2027.

#4154. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.1 livestream reveals a pared-back, four-week update as HoYo plays catch-up

Honkai: Star Rail will continue the Planarcadia story arc in Version 4.1, as the Star Rail Fest presents a new twist.

A new Honkai: Star Rail Special Program has concluded, which means some fresh news about the game’s upcoming major update. Version 4.1, unveiled today as Unraveled for Daybreak, is the action RPG’s next moment, kicking off on March 25.

Unraveled for Daybreak is the next chapter in the ongoing story of Planarcadia, with the Astra Express Crew now invited to a fan fest inspired by their own past journeys. The aptly named Star Rail Fest is ostensibly hosted to allow more of the citizens of Arcadia to experience the Trailblaze.

As everyone’s eyes is fixated on the grand Star Rail Fest, the Phantasmoon Games continue to be in full swing, as does the war with the Supplicants. Star Rail Fest is, however, the big focus of this update, in case it wasn't obvious.

The event is made up of three large-scale zones, each themed around past excursions of the Astral Express. You’ll get to explore the Belobog Zone, Xianzhou Luofu Zone, and Penacony Zone. Later on, you’ll also be able to visit Pearluxe Tower, the headquarters of Pearluxe Corp.

Each area will feature its own attractions, such as the balloon figures of Supreme Guardian Cocolia and the Destruction Engine, the duel against the Lord Ravager Phantylia at Scalegorge Waterscape, and the Pearluxe Tower’s Alloy King Pom-Pom model.

The hot new arrival is bumbling noirish detective Ashveil whom we've met in Version 4.0, and who becomes a playable character with this update. Ashveil is a 5-Star Lightning-Type character, on the Path of The Hunt. You’ll be able to pull for him throughout 4.1's runtime, which is slightly reduced at four weeks instead of the usual six, in order to rebalance the schedule after the extra-long Version 3.8.

In combat, Ashveil is capable of increasing Crit Damage of all allies. He can also mark an enemy as Bait, which reduces the Defence of all enemies on the field so long as this tag holds. If Ashveil uses his Skill on the baited target, he will deal extra Damage and regain Skill Points for the team.

Ashveil can bully that baited target even further by launching Hounding Pursuit. If any of his teammates attacks the Bait, he can further deliver a follow-up attack that gradually accumulates Gluttony for as long as he’s in combat. Gluttony can later be consumed to boost follow-up attack damage.

If he lands a kill, Ashveil continues to deal damage to the next enemy he attacks. That buff is transferred if that enemy is killed. Even in map exploration, Ashveil can be deadly, capable of inflicting Stunned upon enemies within a specific range.

Returning characters this patch will be Hyacine in the first half, and Boothill in the second half. Once again, due to the reduced runtime, their banner reruns will be slightly shorter than normal, at just two weeks each instead of three — so be sure to take that into account if you're planning on pulling for either of them.

Version 4.1 also adds the Wispae War Saga, a new activity where you can practice your leadership skills by commanding different types of Wispae Soldiers in the Graphia Academy. You can upgrade each one, use spell cards to alter their effects, and later face other champions. You ultimately want to play this to unlock new Wispae Companions, not to mention complete the challenges within.

Finally, Version 4.1 marks the start of a new Arcadian Chronicles phase in the Divergent Universe. You’ll be able to use Waypoint Pass cards to explore the different areas. HoYo is also bringing back Planar Fissure and Garden of Plenty with double rewards. And as ever, if you log in for at least seven days after downloading the new patch, you’ll earn 10 premium banner pulls.

#4153. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are, again, for running taxi duty for relatives visiting from overseas. If I had a nickel for every time I had an early morning Gatwick run in tandem with a Sunday Papers post, I’d have two nickels, which isn’t a lot but it’s weird than I’m being paid in USD when I live in the United Kingdom. In that international spirit, here are some fine writings from around the globe.

For Stop Caring, Artemis Octavio interviewed Jeremy Couillard, the multimedia artist behind such offbeat indie experiments as Soul Injector Commando: an FPS about shooting a sense of humanity into enemies based on real-life billionaires.

This past week’s discourse on gamedev team sizes, sparked by a GI.biz post about Star Wars: Galactic Racer and its "core team" of 75, was clearly an inferior rehash of the Nic-sparked Expedition 33 one last year. But it has produced this thoughtful Game Developer piece, by Bryant Francis, on whether we need a new language approach to fit recent developments in outsourcing.

When done right, the model diversifies financial risk and preserves what works about triple-A development without the need to keep everyone under one corporate entity. When done wrong, you can wind up with a game development class system, where creative direction and funding flows in limited directions, and those not lucky enough to be at the center struggle to keep doing the work they love.

This problem is obviously organizational in nature, and not easily fixed by good copyediting. But organizations begin with language, and the language we use to define our work will define the future of video game development.

Writer and former Double Finer Harper Jay considers when games fail. In the interesting 'intent and aspirations' sense, not the tedious 'sales and Steam player counts' sense.

Manhunt’s investment into the stealth simulation is not insignificant, especially for the time. Even with the conceit that there is a snuff director engineering these scenarios, it wants you to understand that there is a world. It behaves largely as you might expect. The rules are mostly the rules of the real worlds. a brick falls because there is "gravity" and it makes "noise" like a normal brick would.

But! There’s rules to the game. Do X and a guard will do Y. Exploiting this is a key to progress and getting high scores. hit a wall, the mook says the thing, he walks over. this is the rule. at least so far.

But this guy doesn’t move. It’s not some meta-textual commentary, it’s not some undercutting trick on the player. He’s just not programmed that way. So I mention it to the game club. something’s up.

This doesn’t work. It doesn’t align. The simulation fails. The artifice is too obvious here. The funhouse is on display a bit too brazenly. It’s endearing maybe in the way that all jank can be. but it’s "off."

Eurogamer’s Robert Purchese meets the man who put a Game Boy Museum into a Game Boy cartridge.

I’ve been learning, as I recommend you do, about the eccentric American moneyman Timothy Dexter (1747-1806), whose preternatural luck in seeing his bumbling investments succeed was matched only by his zest for unhinged wordsmithing. Not really a 'from this week', of course. But then I only heard about the guy on Tuesday after Edwin, mad with fury after years of me editing commas into his articles, sent me Dexter’s punctuation sheet supplement, which he included in reprints of one work “Nowing ones complane of my book the fust edition had no stops”.

I did look around for something BioWare-related to include here, but to be perfectly honest I still think the best eulogy I've read is Edwin's. Even if the first draft needed some commas. Music this week is alternating between Clutch’s gigantic, dive-bombing Wasted Lands, and this SilvaGunner remix of Unbeatable’s best song. Good Sundays, all.

Most things in Version 2.7 follow on from the Hollow Champion competition, which brings together old friends and familiar faces, as well interesting newcomers. Everyone is in it to win some big rewards and earn glory.

Among the unexpected participants the competition has attracted are the Public Security's Metropolitan Order Division, and even some former Calydon's Sweepers. A big challenge that awaits is Black Wolf Romeul, who’s capable of increasing his Crit Damage Resistance and Interruption Resistance by activating a Corruptive Barrier.

Romeul can also cause enemies to continuously lose HP, but you can beat him by putting together a squad that can deal sustained Anomaly damage, which will break through the barrier quickly.

Our first new arrival in Version 2.7 is Cissia of the Metropolitan Order Division. She is an S-Rank Electric Attack Agent who automatically gains three stacks of Venom when she enters the battle. Each stack deals Electric Damage while also increasing her Crit Rate for a time.

When she runs out of Venom, which will happen, Cissia can generate more stacks by using her EX Special Attack. She can also use her Basic Attack, Serpent's Kiss, to better utilise the new stacks of Venom she generates.

The other new Agent may be the more exciting. Nangong Yu, the captain and lead dancer of the Angels of Delusion, can now be part of your team. Nangong Yu is an S-Rank Ether Stun Agent who can boost her team’s Anomaly Buildup Rate against Stunned enemies.

Being part of an idol group has its perks, because she automatically regenerates Downbeat as time goes on, and even more any time a squad member inflicts an enemy with Anomaly. Nangong Yu can then use Downbeat - after enough has been accumulated - on charged attacks that keep enemies stunned for longer. Her Ultimate triggers Ether Veil: Delusion Reprise, which boosts the entire squad’s Attack.

Returning Agents in Version 2.7 will be Yidhari, the S-Rank Ice Rupture Agent, as well as Seed, the Electric Attack Agent.

Outside of all the very important action in the core story, this chapter also brings new themed events to Lumina Square’s Simmer Hot Pot Restaurant. The Simulated Battle Trial is also getting some love, with updated mechanics and new enemy line-ups.

Catch up on our recently updated Zenless Zone Zero character tier list, and don’t forget to check out these Zenless Zone Zero codes before you jump in for some free stuff.

#4150. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel Is Reportedly Still "More Than Two Years Away"

After initially announcing The Elder Scrolls 6 all the way back in 2018, Bethesda has now officially confirmed its subtitle: Sentinel. Ooh.

However, if you're under the impression that this means the game is somewhat imminent, a new post from Bloomberg's Jason Schreier suggests that it is still "more than two years away" (thanks, Push Square).

I think a lot of people forget that The Elder Scrolls VI was only announced in 2018 (along with Starfield) to soften the blow of Fallout 76 — "Don't worry, even though we're making a multiplayer game we've got single-player stuff coming too!" Sorry to say this game is still more than 2 years away!

This, of course, would likely mean that its eventual release will land at least a decade following the game's announcement at E3 2018, which is frankly just ridiculous. And we thought the eight-year wait for Metroid Prime 4: Beyond was overkill.

It's just yet another indication that studios need to exercise some restraint when it comes to early announcements. As Schreier stated in his post, Bethesda seemingly wanted to balance out its Fallout 76 announcement with the promise of another single player-focused Elder Scrolls game, but we're not convinced anybody could have predicted what a long wait it would turn out to be.

Nintendo is pretty good at keeping its announcements under lock and key until the right moment these days, and we suspect that Prime 4 proved a big lesson for the company in this regard. Hell, Zelda: Ocarina of Time was only properly announced in June this year, and it's launching tomorrow at the time of writing. Can't argue with that!

#4149. Mass Effect 5 was named Universe partly because it let players generate alternate timelines based on their choices in previous entries, technical director says

The system was part of BioWare's effort to give the player "absolute autonomy", according to Romain Toutain

In case you missed it, an internal trailer for the new Mass Effect game which BioWare were working on prior to EA shutting them down hit the net late last week. It offered a peek at what the studio were cooking with this new entry, dubbed Mass Effect Universe. According to its technical director, one of the reasons the game was given that name was that it had a system aimed at letting players form alternate timelines based on their choices in previous Mass Effects.

Romain Toutain, BioWare's franchise technical director since 2022, said as much during a Twitch stream that saw him react to the leaked trailer. The on-demand version of this steam looks like it may since have been yanked, but not before a BlueSky user with the handle @loustica-lucia went through, took some clips, and added subtitles translating Toutain as he chats about the trailer in French.

"All the choices made in the first Mass Effect games were taken into account," the developer said after the trailer finished. "One of the reasons why it was called Mass Effect Universe is that you had so many choices that you could plug your saves together to create parallel universes. To keep it simple. It’s not exactly how it worked. You had different timelines, basically. You could almost generate timelines, kinda like Zero Time [Dilemma]."

So earlier, my brother was watching Octobinz (Romain Toutain)'s livestream on Twitch. He was the Technical Director on Mass Effect Universe, so I wanted to share some bits he discussed. As he speaks french, I added subtitles to make it more accessible for everyone! #MassEffect #MassEffectUniverse[image or embed]

Asked if it was similar to Dragon Age Keep, the service BioWare set up to let folks create world states based on their Dragon Age: Origins and Dragon Age 2 choices that they could then import into Inquisition, Toutain said "kinda". Though, he stressed that this Mass Effect system worked in some extra complexity by letting players make decisions that might contradict things they've previously done.

"Everything in the game, everything was stateful," the dev explained. "At any time, you could stop the game - I mean, you could pause it - and ask a system that solved logical equations, ‘Is this valid?’ And if it isn’t valid, what conditions must be met for it to be valid? For the game to set these conditions. And if the content doesn’t exist, then we know the content doesn’t exist, so we’ll either have to create another branch, either that, or we know we have to create the content.

"So, if you killed a guy, and you needed that guy for your mission, the game will make sure you can complete the mission. Or, if that’s what the designers have decided, well, no, the mission’s failed because you killed that guy. Or else, something that was bound to happen doesn’t happen, just so that a path remains open, so that you can get around the problem." Toutain summed the system up as being something that was "difficult to set up", but worked well.

It certainly sounds ambitious, if a lot of work to get right. Whether it and the pursuit of giving the player "absolute autonomy" which the dev says it was part of would've made Mass Effect 5 a return to form for BioWare is up for debate and will likely remain so forever unless someone swoops in to perform a miracle resurrection pretty sharpish. Personally, it at least sounds like something that'd have piqued my curiosity enough to see what Shep and co were up to, despite not being the biggest Mass Effecter.

#4148. Heartopia goes to the movies with its next event

Heartopia's Whale Island will soon host a new event that's all about the magic of cinema.

Heartopia’s next in-game event has been announced, and it’s one you may not have seen coming. Developer XD Games revealed Dreamlight Cinematics Festival, an upcoming limited-time event that celebrates cinema and movie-making.

Dreamlight Cinematics kicks off March 21, and will run through May 1, available across the game’s PC and mobile versions.

Dreamlight Cinematics Festival takes place on Whale Island. And, perhaps as an unofficial Oscars tie-in, it’s all about classic Hollywood filmmaking. Not only that, it also celebrates the aesthetics and industrial design of that era.

All around the game’s world, you’ll be able to find festival-themed collectables, which you can then use to unlock free Time-Limited Exhibition Passes.

If you log in during the event’s runtime, you’ll get the Car Cinema furniture set for free. This cosmetic bundle comes with chairs that are modelled after vintage vehicles, as well as poster display stands with unique movie making-themed decorations.

If you’re looking to spend some money, the Deluxe Festival Pack comes with a large Island Sunset Billboard, which you can place outside your home so everyone knows you spent that money. The same pack also comes with the Popcorn Movie Ticket chat bubble skin, and a 10% bonus to Festival Tokens when you sell stuff at the store.

Regardless of which pack you get, you’ll earn collection points for each, which puts you on the path to unlocking outfits like the Dreamlight Cinematics Festival-specific Modern Show Dandy and Modern Show Belle. There’s also a Cinematic Moments building material set launching with this event.

#4147. 32-year-old "ellipsoid" horror game Ecstatica gets a PC re-release today, showing us an alternative timeline in which polygonal 3D never became dominant

One of my favourite hobbies is digging up older pieces of gaming tech or software know-how and asking myself: "man, what would the world have been like, if every GPU were made out of Gorgonzola?" Or less silly words to that effect. Nostalgia aside, it's useful to revisit historical alternatives in the face of very rich people who would have us believe that only their trillion-dollar boondoggle is "the" future.

The code running 1994 horror game Ecstatica probably isn't going to topple Unreal Engine anytime soon, but look at this article's header image, and tell me you aren't fascinated. Why is everything so… pert? I will tell you why: Ecstatica's graphics make heavy use of ellipsoids. They're the basis for everything from werewolf buttocks to the grain of castle flagstones. You can experience this terrifying bubble-wrap reality for yourself in today's Steam and GOG re-release of both Ecstatica and its sequel, care of SNEG Games.

I myself know about Ecstatica thanks to Jasper Byrne, developer of the brilliant Lone Survivor, whom I spoke to yonks ago about "de-making" and monolithic progress narratives. Byrne mentioned it as an example of a road-not-taken in videogame graphics production and aesthetics. Or at least, a road-not-taken-very-far.

Created by Andrew Spencer Studios, Ecstatica uses ellipsoids with actual volumes for characters, most objects, and much of the environment - all of it running on the CPU. It schlops and schlurps the ellipsoids together into more complex, rounded masses. Look at the slightly nauseating ovoid grit of those dungeon walls. It's like somebody wallpapered their kid's bedroom with xenomorph eggs. Ugh, I'm getting Yedoma Globula flashbacks.

As such, Ecstatica cuts against what would become the dominant trend of using polygons for 3D visuals, though the game's engine is capable of rendering polygons for square or flat objects such as doors and crosses. As for what you actually do, in this appallingly bulbous simulation: you are an unfortunate wanderer who's strayed into a village full of monsters. There are many ways to die. Released two years before the original Resident Evil, Ecstatica is an early example of fixed-perspective survival horror, splintering off from adventure games. It's puzzle-driven with a lot of "absurd British humour", as the Steam and GOG storepages for the re-release explain.

I'm not sure who exactly worked on this port, but publishers SNEG were founded in 2020 by former GOG staffers, with the goal of restoring or, at least, republishing and resurfacing various forgotten PC games. The Ecstatica rebuild includes controller support and three graphics modes, changeable on the fly: one for the original DOS version of the game, one for the 1997 re-release on Windows 95, and a "real-time high resolution render". I'm not sure if any of the original devs are involved - they broke up after Ecstatica 2, midway through development of their third game Urban Decay. The latter was also ellipsoid-based, but the devs switched to a more familiar polygonal look before the project ran out of gas.

#4146. All the hype has already made Crimson Desert one of the biggest launches on Steam this year

We're merely days away from the end of the first quarter of 2026, and Crimson Desert has come in clutch to join the list of big sellers.

Crimson Desert, the open-world action RPG off-shoot from Korean MMO Black Desert Online, has officially launched, nearly six years after it was initially revealed. The game has been building up a lot of momentum over the years, which recently coalesced to turn it into one of 2026’s most anticipated titles.

All of it has been leading up to this moment, and the game appears to have landed smoothly, though not without controversy, as has seemingly become part of its MO.

It has not been 24 hours since Crimson Desert launched on PC and consoles, and it’s already become a big hit. On Steam, one of two stores where the game can be purchased (the other being the Epic Games Store), the game shot to the top of the charts.

The action RPG continued to accumulate more and more players on Steam, peaking at a very respectable 239,045 concurrent players (via SteamDB). Though its success was very much expected, we perhaps didn’t predict its peak would be that high.

Indeed, Crimson Desert has been in Steam’s top 100 global sellers list for six weeks, jumping up six spots to become the number one seller this week just before it launched. As we get closer to the weekend, the numbers could climb even higher.

This peak concurrent puts Crimson Desert in the same league as several of the other major releases of the first quarter of 2026. The top spot continues to belong to Slay the Spire 2, which peaked at a staggering 574,638 concurrent players. It happened just days after the juggernaut Resident Evil Requiem achieved its own 344,214 peak concurrent, which was the year’s highest up until Slay the Spire 2’s release. All three are well ahead of Nioh 3’s 88,045 peak concurrent, and Marathon’s nearly identical peak of 88,337.

Crimson Desert has seen something of a mixed reception by critics. James gave it three stars in our review, saying it “lacks the connective sinew to be truly functional,” which is a common criticism shared by other outlets. Many also lamented the sheer number of systems fighting for player attention, its poorly explained mechanics, and counterintuitive controls.

On Steam, at least, players have similarly been divided, with the current Steam user rating sitting at Mixed, based on 8,728 reviews. Unsurprisingly, most of the negative reactions fall on the clunky controls and the game’s tendency to, as one Steam user put it, “so miserably tries to be everything at once, and fails to be anything at all.”

#4144. Feature: 25 Years Later, How Many Of These Original Xbox Launch Titles Have You Played?

From the original North American launch on November 15, 2001

Welcome to the month of Xbox's 25th anniversary! Xbox will be celebrating that milestone officially on November 15th, but before we get there, we thought we'd use the chance to highlight the very first games that ever launched on Xbox.

To do that, we're going back to the initial list of North American Xbox launch titles, of which there were 20 in all. Some of them are obvious standouts, such as Halo: Combat Evolved, Fuzion Frenzy, Dead or Alive 3 and Project Gotham Racing, while others are more obscure - Arctic Thunder, Dark Summit, Mad Dash Racing, etc.

Here's the full list of all 20 launch titles:

Now, of course, some of these games are still playable to this day on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, while others have always remained locked to the original Xbox. The likes of Project Gotham Racing, Shrek and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x are highly-requested additions to the Xbox backwards compatibility library, but it seems unlikely they'll ever make the cut at this point - almost certainly due to licensing reasons.

However, you may not know that games like Cel Damage and Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee are still playable to this day on modern consoles, and they're still well worth checking out despite their age.

So, how many of these original Xbox launch titles have you played? Let us know down in the comments section below, and please do give us your recommendations with some of the obscure ones - NHL Hitz is still one of my faves!

#4143. Crimson Desert's first patch aims at fixing controls, but it mostly affects mouse and keyboard

The first post-launch patch for Crimson Desert is here, and the list of changes is promising, even if it doesn't go far enough to address some deeper issues.

Crimson Desert has been out for a few days now, and as positive as its been received by many players, the game suffers from several fundamental issues that anyone who’s played it has called out.

Perhaps the loudest one of those has been how the game controls, which is a problem that stems from the complexity of controls themselves, as well as the underlying animations behind many of the actions the player character performs.

In the first case, at least, something is being done.

Developer Pearl Abyss rolled out patch 1.00.03 for Crimson Desert on Monday. The patch is available now on Steam and PlayStation, with Xbox and the Epic Games Store following “at a later time.”

Today’s update follows a letter to players the developer issued on Saturday. The letter generally acknowledged player feedback, but specifically pointed to complaints about the game’s clunky controls as something of a focus for the team.

The action RPG has actually broken its launch peak concurrent player numbers over the weekend, though only by a few thousands more. Its Steam user review rating has also improved over the same period.

This latest update only includes an initial set of fixes, but Pearl Abyss vowed to keep working on addressing all other points of feedback. A highlight in 1.00.03 is the addition of a Storage at Howling Hill Camp, which can be used to store inventory items.

The most important changes, of course, affect how the game controls on keyboard and mouse. Pearl Abyss included several fixes and altered some of the default presets to make the experience less painful when playing the game with a keyboard and mouse.

There are sadly no changes to controllers, but it is something that the developer said we can expect to see in future patches. More improvements for keyboard and mouse setups are in the works, too.

Beyond the control changes, patch 1.00.03 also includes a set of gameplay tweaks, especially when it comes to enemy health and difficulty. It also makes fast travelling more convenient, and brings a few fixes to NPC dialogue. You can read the full change log on Steam.

If you’re deep in Crimson Desert already, we definitely recommend giving our guides a look. We recently added new pages to help you figure out where to socket your Abyss Gear, how to find Contribution Points - and where to spend them, as well as more generally helpful information like how to expand your inventory, and how to reveal the map.

#4142. Review: The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

You’re not ready for this. No matter how many trailers you’ve watched or how much pre-release footage you’ve pored over, walking out into Hyrule Field for the first time in the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a revelatory experience.

It’s easy to forget how impactful Hyrule Field really was in the N64 original. While the game itself is still held in remarkably high regard, its main hub world has arguably been supplanted by later entries, particularly Breath of the Wild's enormous, immersive open world. It’s pioneering, yes, but it’s also quite small and empty when viewed through a modern lens.

The remake, with its breathtaking visuals, modernised controls, and revamped soundtrack, makes it feel new again. Standing at the entrance to Kokiri Forest and panning the camera around to soak in all of the details, I had to take a beat to stop myself being overcome by the enormity of the moment.

Making everything feel new again is really at the heart of the Switch 2 remake. I want to be clear: this is basically the same game, but Nintendo has tweaked just enough to make it feel fresh. Whether it’s the slightly different chest location for the Kokiri Sword or the Cucco hiding spots in Kakariko Village, there will always be something — however small — to give you pause.

The biggest change is the visuals. Much like Star Fox, Ocarina of Time is a staggering upgrade over the original, offering an almost overwhelming amount of detail across the board. From the small trinkets on Link’s tunic (who, by the way, is definitively 'Link' here, with no renaming options) to the way shards of broken pots stay on the ground and move underfoot, every aspect has been overhauled to take advantage of Switch 2’s power.

Yet despite the almost hyperrealistic visuals, it retains the original's spirit. There was a lot of discourse about the presentation when the remake was first properly revealed, particularly around characters’ faces. Any doubts about the approach will fade away as soon as you start playing. Everything looks right; whether it’s Link’s design or Zora's Domain, this is Ocarina of Time through and through. If you’re one of the many fans who were hoping to see the Spaceworld 2000 and Wii U tech demos properly realised, this is it and more.

The visual upgrades extend to the dungeons, of course, and it's crazy how impactful they are on your enjoyment. Inside the Deku Tree feels like a living world with realistic bark walls and copious spider webs. Likewise, the shimmering reflections and ethereal soundtrack completely transform the Water Temple. Despite minimal changes to the gameplay and structure — minor alterations to puzzles ultimately have little impact — the dungeons are a joy to explore once again.

It’s not all perfect, though. Keeping such a stunning game running at 60fps on a handheld takes some jiggery-pokery, and Nintendo's solution has resulted in a few visual blemishes. Assets in the distance — mountains and trees — look overly smooth and there’s some shimmering going on when you pan the camera around. It’s nowhere near as severe as Xenoblade Chronicles X on Switch 2, but it’s definitely something you’ll notice occasionally, particularly during handheld play.

Overall resolution takes a notable hit undocked, too, to the point where even Link himself can look a little fuzzy at times. It definitely needs mentioning, although it wasn't significantly detrimental to my experience. Keeping the game running smoothly feels like the more important priority, and Nintendo has nailed that aspect.

The audio has also been completely revamped, as well. The soundtrack, while familiar, has been reworked with new orchestral renditions, and everything from the Kokiri Forest track to the final, epic battle sounds incredible. Key cutscenes also feature voice acting, and it's some of the best I've heard from a first-party Nintendo game in quite some time. Your fairy companion Navi, whose in-game interruptions have been drastically cut down, is delightfully cheerful.

Exploring Hyrule and taking in the new visuals is made all the more satisfying thanks to the new control scheme. I’ve mentioned panning the camera around a couple of times, but it’s worth stressing that full camera control is completely new - a strange thing to highlight in 2026, but the ability to properly absorb everything this world has to offer really enhances your relationship with it. You feel so much more involved, and it helps that locations like Hyrule Castle Town have been upgraded to take advantage: no more pre-rendered backgrounds, you can now soak in all of the glorious detail.

The other major addition is the ability to jump whenever you please. Again, how quaint! Yet leaping at the press of a button gives you so much more autonomy over Link’s movements, even if it doesn’t open new routes or opportunities during your quest. You still jump at the same moments to scale platforms and solve puzzles, but doing it yourself without having to run off a ledge to trigger it is both quicker and more satisfying.

Combat feels comfortingly familiar: you lock onto your enemy and slash at them with ‘Y’, altering the direction of your swing by tilting the left analogue stick. You can hop about, perform a backwards somersault, and execute a leaping attack with either ‘X’ (the default jump button) or ‘A’, while holding and releasing ‘Y’ triggers the spin attack. It’s basically the same – why fix what isn’t broken, right?

Yet every attack now lands with such ferocity — accompanied by a searing red flash and a deafening crash — that combat feels completely overhauled. Again, old is new. Indeed, it’s so effective that it even makes Tears of the Kingdom's clashes feel comparatively tame.

Making use of your various weapons and items is also much easier than before. By holding down ‘R’, you’ll bring up an item inventory that instantly looks familiar if you’ve played TOTK or Echoes of Wisdom. Displayed in a single line, you quickly scroll left and right for your weapon of choice, whether it be a Deku Stick, a Bombchu, or the Megaton Hammer. The selection is relatively limited compared to, say, Echoes of Wisdom, so I never felt the UI was unwieldy or overwhelming; I always found what I was looking for straight away.

Meanwhile, key items like the Ocarina, masks, and Iron Boots are mapped to the D-pad. The latter is especially useful in the Water Temple, which gained its reputation as a major sticking point partly due to the need to repeatedly access the main menu to equip and unequip the boots. Tapping down on the D-pad is a lot more intuitive and makes for a breezier experience.

You can also do this for the newly-designed Lenses of Truth, which function exactly as the original Lens of Truth but have been revamped as a pair of goggles instead of a magnifying glass. It makes so much more sense!

The game is littered with similar tweaks, many of which have a noticeable quality-of-life impact. Reloading now drops you in the exact location you last saved (instead of at your house as Young Link and the Temple of Time as Adult Link). Elsewhere, the new Echo Gem, a reward from the House of Skulltula quest that replaces the Stone/Shard of Agony, shines and vibrates as you approach any Gold Skulltulas.

As for the Ocarina, you can play tunes in a variety of ways, the most basic of which is by simply pressing specific inputs via the face and shoulder buttons. Holding down ‘ZL’ brings up a menu of songs you’ve learned so far - handy for a quick reminder at any given moment.

However, you can also use the Switch 2’s built-in mic to input tunes using your own voice. Simply hum the tune you want and it’ll mostly pick it up with no fuss. You have the option to practice tunes if you wish, and it makes for a cute, if gimmicky way to use the Ocarina.

I’ve not been able to test Hori’s Electric Ocarina (and who knows where Nintendo’s official instrument is at), but I whipped out my guitar to test a few songs, and lo and behold, it actually worked. It certainly won’t be my go-to method, and chances are I’ll just stick to the buttons, but it’s neat.

I've not been able to test the Zelda Notes features during the review period, but you might find it a worthwhile addition if you're keen to create and share Ocarina songs. If you have some Zelda-themed amiibo lying about, tapping one during gameplay yields a few bonus items (arrows, recovery hearts, bombs, etc.), but thankfully nothing that could be deemed essential. All welcome additions, though.

What hasn’t been added for the remake is the Master Quest, and this is a real bummer. Available via a special GameCube release and as an unlockable in the 3DS remake, Master Quest proved an excellent way for veterans to test their skills upon completing the game. Given how closely the Switch 2 remake sticks to the core structure of the original, veterans will breeze through with minimal issues. And if you do ever get stuck, the new Threads of Time feature, which essentially documents your progress, will help you get back on track.

I died just once during the entire journey because I just got caught off-guard by an Iron Knuckle in the Spirit Temple. You can increase the difficulty slightly by altering the UI to show either minimal information or no information at all, but it’s no replacement for the changes that Master Quest could have brought. I'm hopeful that it will be added via an update, but it’s a glaring omission.

The lack of multiple save files is also disappointing. Yes, you can just create additional profiles at a system level, but the game allows you just one manual save along with several autosaves. Sometimes you just want to experience the start of the game again without impacting your main save file, so this is a shame.

The one last major addition is The Hall of Fallen Foes, and this is a cool, albeit inconsequential bonus. Accessed by sleeping in a bed after a specific campaign moment, here you can gaze upon statues based on enemies you’ve slain. It’s a lovely way to properly appreciate their updated designs, and you’re also given the opportunity to replay boss fights or even take on multiple bosses in succession. The rewards for doing so are useless, but the act of optimising your battles and beating your time is fun enough on its own.

And so, even with all that knowledge, you're really not ready for this. The visuals, the gameplay, the audio – everything has been thoughtfully upgraded to such a degree that this will completely replace the original for many. While the lack of Master Quest means it falls short of being definitive, it's still a remarkable remake, and a must-buy for Switch 2.

Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the experience with stunning visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio. Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time.

That said, it is a very safe remake. Despite lots of minor changes throughout, it’s still essentially the same game you’ve likely already played, and so you might find it offers little challenge if you’re familiar with the N64 original or 3DS remake. This makes the lack of Master Quest — or really any kind of hard mode — particularly glaring, but I’m hopeful it’ll be added in the future.

Just want to point out that I feel pretty confident that we would have possibly the same level of vitriole (maybe from the other side of the argument?) if this score had been a 10/10. It feels like every time this site or IGN releases a perfect score, they are criticized for being corporate shills, Nintendoters, lazy reviewers, etc. So, let's please be respectful and kind, take a couple breaths, and try to have some perspective. I know it can be frustrating to feel like your favorite/beloved [blank] isn't getting the appreciation or glory or credibility you feel it deserves - I was hoping for a 10 here, too! - but it doesn't have to take anything away from the enjoyment of it. I guarantee you are not alone with your love and passion for these media. But let's also try to understand that we - the people writing these reviews, included - are all individuals with subjective points-of-view. Everyone else's opinions are just as valid as your own. #4141. Skyrim's Successor Finally Re-Revealed as The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel

It's official: The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is the full title of Bethesda's next open world RPG.

The subtitle has been announced as part of the developer's 40th anniversary celebrations. Confirmation comes via a very brief trailer at the end of the company's new video, which you can watch below.

The teaser shows sand blowing across an Elder Scroll, and it concludes with an ominous quote from Yazar, a Moth Priest (remember them from Oblivion?) in service of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell.

It reads: "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate."

Obviously not, but the teaser and subtitle reveal nail down at least one thing: this game's going to take place in Sentinel, which is both a capital city and kingdom within Hammerfell — the home of the Redguards.

You can expect deserts, ancient ruins, and an adventure-filled coastline.

When we'll actually get to see The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is anyone's guess at this point. Bethesda has just warned that "it’ll be some time before we’re ready to share more". The wait continues...

Are you feeling excited for this next Elder Scrolls game? Brave the desert of the comments section below.

Robert (or Rob if you're lazy) is an assistant editor of Push Square, and has been a fan of PlayStation since the 90s, when Tekken 2 introduced him to the incredible world of video games. He still takes his fighting games seriously, but RPGs are his true passion. The Witcher, Persona, Dragon Quest, Mass Effect, Final Fantasy, Trails, Tales — he's played 'em all. A little too much, some might say.

#4140. Clean a whole planet with a toothbrush in Moon Sweepers, the PowerWash genre's latest crime against perfectionists

I don't much go for PowerWash Simulator-likes, but there is something appealingly unwholesome about a game in which you have to wipe the dust off an entire moon. Using a toothbrush. True, you can upgrade to beefier hoovering equipment in Moon Sweepers by cashing in shipments of lunar dirt, but that strikes me as a dangerous concession to brute mass production thinking – it risks consigning centuries of artisanal knowledge to, well, the dustbin.

Take pride in your craft, colleagues! If we become over-reliant on hoover-me-dos, we'll lose the skill of cleansing celestial objects by hand, and sooner or later, they'll give our jobs to the bots. You can keep your new-fangled vacuum mops. If anybody needs me, I'll be over here in the Sea of Tranquility, collecting individual motes with a pair of tweezers.

Moon Sweepers is the work of DragDrop Games, a two-person team who are now busting their chops patching the game after a surprisingly popular launch on Friday. To expand a little on the self-explanatory title, the game sees you placing depots near cleaning sites and tracking your overall progress by way of a big holographic globe back at base.

I'm not sure I have the patience to polish an entire moon, but I am certainly salivating over the delicious grey, chunky-edged plateaus left behind by the sweepers in the trailer. In general, Moon Sweepers has me thinking anew about a possible subgenre of game dedicated to cleaning up the messes left behind by players of other games. What, you really think they just "de-spawn" the corpses in Counter-Strike? Nonsense! Somebody has to come in and tidy all that shit up, surely.

Moon Sweepers has multiplayer support for up to 16, and you can seemingly spend a whole session doing low-G flips in a curiously municipal Apollo buggy... if you're an absolute disgrace to the profession. Mind you, even your starry-eyed Evil Knievel impressions will scrape away moonpowder. There is ultimately no escape from your role as lunar janitor.

I just pray for whoever appoints themselves manager of a full 16 player moonsweeping operation. At least there are no enemies to worry about - just lashings of aeons-old asteroid powder. No, you cannot lie in the stuff and make moondust angels, which seems a ghastly oversight. Read more on Steam.

#4139. Stalker 2’s first expansion officially revealed, and it's taking us to the power plant where it all began

Stalker 2’s first add-on isn’t far off, and it may just be the thing to bring you back to post-apocalyptic Chornobyl in 2026.

One of the biggest reveals out of today’s Xbox Partner Preview showcase has been the new Stalker 2 expansion. The developer did tease some sort of announcement ahead of the event, but I don’t think an expansion was on many of our bingo cards.

Cost of Hope is the big news; a new add-on that the developer has wisely decided to reveal fairly close to release. Or, at least, the planned release target.

First off, Cost of Hope is set for release this summer. It’ll arrive on all current platforms simultaneously, meaning PC, Xbox, and PlayStation. The expansion is described as “non-linear”, and it takes place in the heartlands, deeper into the Zone.

The story revolves around a conflict between Duty, and Freedom, two factions whose idea of the what the Zone is and their understanding of its possibilities differ widely. You’ll be playing as protagonist Skif once again, and the expansion’s events will run parallel to the main game.

GSC Game World says Cost of Hope will introduce two new regions, offering dozens of hours of gameplay. We’ll get to actually explore the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant as part of the expansion, alongside the Iron Forest.

Each of the two new regions will have its own hub area, NPCs, quests, activities and stories. Of course, it wouldn’t be a Stalker expansion without some new weapons, and Cost of Hope promises a few - some can even be seen in the trailer.

The developer also confirmed that there’s one other story DLC in the works. Together with Heart of Chornobyl, and Cost of Hope all three will form a trilogy of interconnected stories. More details on Cost of Hope - including a release date - will be revealed sometime in the summer.

#4138. "IT FLIPS UP," Fallout New Vegas modders yell after releasing a funky Pip-Boy based on cancelled entry Van Buren's design docs

The same folks are hard at work remaking Van Buren as part of a project dubbed Fallout: The New West

One of the days last week was October 23rd. It's the date in the Fallout universe when the bombs dropped and has morphed into a time for yearly community happenings plus, in Bethesda's case, usually some marketing. Sometimes, modders behind long-running projects time up standalone releases with it, as has been the case this year with the folks behind Fallout: The New West, the project aiming to make their own version of Black Isle Studios' cancelled third Fallout game. They've released a few guns inspired by the canned entry, which you may know by its codename Van Buren, but the headliner from this gear drop for New Vegas is a funky new Pip-Boy design.

According to its creators, this Lil Pip 3000 iteration of Fallout's iconic wrist-mounted computer has been recreated based on Van Buren's original design docs. Worn by inmates in Tibbets Prison, the AI overlord-run slammer that the modders have already recreated for a demo of their Van Buren remake, the Lil Pip has made its way to Mojave in the hands of an unnamed ranger who's deposited it near Nipton.

It does all the standard Pip-Boy things and should work with a host of established mods which add extra features to The Courier's fancy bracelet. Most importantly of all, thanks to custom animations, the lid flips up when you whip the device out to use it. To be clear since the modders have emphasised this in all caps, I said "IT FLIPS UP". In all seriousness, it's a cool design that departs from the general blockiness of the default Pip-Boys worn by Fallout protagonists old and new. It's perhaps heavier on children's toy vibes than its siblings, but not to the extent I'd say it looks like it couldn't survive its wearer failing to step out of the way of a rogue missile or grenade.

Alongside it, the New West lot have released a Wattz Weapon Pack. Consisting of five laser guns in the classic Fallout style, including a freshly assembled burst pistol from Van Buren, the mod also includes custom animations and add-ons to help these new energy weapons fit in seamlessly with the rest of New Vegas' arsenal. They'll even be distributed throughout the Capital Wasteland if you're running the Tale of Two Wastelands mod which mashes New Vegas and Fallout 3's worldspaces together.

If you fancy nabbing either mod, you'll need to nab a fair few requirements. The New Vegas Script Extender, JIP LN NVSE Plugin, JohnnyGuitar NVSE, and kNVSE Animation Plugin are musts for both, while the weapon pack also needs the Gun Runners’ Arsenal DLC, ShowOff xNVSE Plugin, ISControl Enabler, and Sound Extender.

#4137. Never one to lag behind HSR and ZZZ, Genshin Impact will introduce its own new pink-haired animal-themed girl in Version Luna 6

Plus Mondstadt is expanding yet further north in Genshin Impact's Luna 6 update.

Today’s Genshin Impact Special Program has wrapped up, and it’s brought us some big news about the next major update. Luna 6 is the next phase in the action RPG’s story, titled Song of the Welkin Moon: Rondo - Augured Homecoming.

It’s set to arrive on April 8, bringing with it a tonne of new content, including a big expansion to the original region of Mondstadt.

As part of this new update, Mondstadt’s northern parts expand with new areas. The new Dornman Port is one thing, but the most exciting is the Temple of Space. This floating structure is home to Asmoday fragments, and is made up of different realms inspired by Liyue, Sumeru, and various other civilizations from around Teyvat. Launching with the update is a new mechanic that lets you manipulate the space to reveal hidden paths containing secrets.

If you take the time to explore, you’ll find a lot to there to learn about Asmoday, Ruler of Space. There’s a new boss to take on in the temple, too: Watcher: Fallen Vigil.

The only new character in Luna 6 is Linnea, who continues the current trend within HoYoverse games of focussing heavily on cute pink-haired animal-themed girls. Linnea is a 5-Star Geo Bow user who can really work with parties made up of Lunar-Crystallize characters, with her big gimmick being the ability to turn Hydro-Crystallize reactions into Lunar-Crystallize reactions.

Linnea has a companion, Lumi, who allows her to increase the Lunar-Crystallize damage she deals, while also lowering her enemies’ Geo resistance. Linnea can also deliver either off-field Geo damage or a Lunar-Crystallize reaction hit with her Elemental Skill.

Beyond that, she can heal the party using her Elemental Burst. If you take Linnea with you as you explore, she can help you discover rare animals, thanks to her innate naturalist abilities.

This update will also see Chasca get her first-ever rerun, and you’ll be able to roll for her in the first phase of Event Wishes. The second phase will feature no new characters and instead focus on Nefer and Lauma. There’s going to be another Chronicled Wish banner, this time specifically for Fontaine characters.

You can look forward to a few other new arrivals in Luna 6, including The Nod-Krai Trade Expo, some quality of life updates to Miliastra Wonderland to up the number of players in each lobby, not to mention various other UI changes.

#4136. OG Xbox Game 'Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee' Gets Remastered, But What Do The Critics Think?

Was it worth digging the original Xbox title back up?

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee launched on the original Xbox in 2003, a few months after its GameCube debut, and sadly, only in North America. The kaiju arena-brawler, which depicted the iconic King of Monsters, Godzilla, body-slamming Ghidorah into various cityscapes, has apparently made a big enough impact to warrant Atari funding a remaster in 2026.

Sadly, the whole North American release made it quite difficult for us Brits to get our mucky mitts on the game, and DAMM wasn't a big enough deal for Xbox to share the game with the rest of the world. DAMM did get the backward compatibility treatment, however, only on Xbox 360, and again restricted to North America.

I guess then, we're quite pleased Atari decided to take a punt on a DAMM remaster. Even though it seems to share many of the original's downfalls, Godzilla's WWE antics are going to be available on November 3rd on Xbox Series X|S, and best of all, I can play it from my lovely little home in Cornwall.

So, here's what the critics are saying about Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered:

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered brings the classic kaiju brawler roaring back with impressive rebuilt visuals, satisfying arena destruction, and chaotic multiplayer battles. While its limited roster and tedious character unlocks feel dated, the accessible combat and faithful Godzilla presentation make this a thoroughly entertaining return for the King of the Monsters."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like a new game with its graphical upgrade, held back slightly by a lack of any other meaningful new additions and a somewhat grindy gameplay loop."

"Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed."

Review Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is at its best when it simulates the idea of smashing kaiju toys together as a kid in short sessions with friends, and at its worst when it attempts to prolong a game that never had much depth to begin with. The result is a remaster I’m glad exists considering the drought of Godzilla brawlers, but with a few caveats–not to mention the sting of realizing that the original GameCube and Xbox game were absent of arbitrary grinding."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered remains goofy fun, and Atari’s remaster looks and runs well. It’s still a rather simple game and probably not the most comprehensive when it comes to the characters and lore. But it’s a good time and offers quite a few different modes to get acclimated and beat up famous faces."

"Right now, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a great version of a good retro game. Because the game was remade from the ground up, I wish the developers had made a super version of the Godzilla trilogy with more content. While Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered’s combat is really fun, there’s not much depth. There are lots of modes, and a bit of RPG unlocking, but this isn’t a deep fighting game that’s going to be played at tournaments. It’s a great budget buy for Godzilla fans. But more content would have made Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered a more obvious recommendation. If you’re at all curious, or have any fondness for the original game, it remains a fun time."

"In the media shadow of sacred monsters like Grand Theft Auto VI and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, only an equally fearless monstrosity could face them: Godzilla. Nearly a quarter century after its release on GameCube, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee returns with a remaster that discreetly refreshes the audiovisual experience and improves the progression without betraying its structure. The core is that of a 3D fighting game in which kaiju clashes are accompanied by the destruction of entire cities, in a blaze of explosions and particle effects. Behind this chaos lies a combat system that's immediate, but not always precise and balanced, suspended somewhere between classic fighting games and the festive jumble of a party game. The mechanics are simple, despite a certain unwieldiness in the movements, and the best of the action is found especially in local multiplayer."

Well, there you have it, folks! Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is an almost perfect example of a good '7' rated game. At the time of writing, the remaster is holding down a 72 score on Metacritic.

What's interesting is that the original Xbox release scored 73 on Metacritic - a single point higher than the remaster. It's funny how 23 years can pass and a game can be reviewed almost identically.
